nodes.name: Player input and body orientation
nodes.purpose: Turns keyboard and mouse intent into movement actions, strafing, turn deltas, walk and sneak toggles, target facing and the camera-relative run lean.

nodes.name: Character movement and vertical states
nodes.purpose: Advances the character every update: animation-derived displacement, step-up and ground stick, slope slide, jump and climb selection, blocked-move recovery, water wading and the dive timer.

nodes.name: Orbit and first-person camera
nodes.purpose: Runs the third-person orbit, normalized zoom, collision pull-in and close-wall lift, pitch clamps, look-back preset and the first-person eye.

nodes.name: Animation selection and root motion
nodes.purpose: Chooses locomotion and combat clips from movement mode and weapon stance, samples root-bone translation as movement, evaluates attack combo windows and feeds the locomotion sampler that turns animation time into a displacement.

nodes.name: Damage and mitigation rules
nodes.purpose: Computes melee, ranged and fall damage, applies armour protection, resolves talent rolls, glancing blows and the minimum damage floor, and reads the gravity and fall state that feed impact damage.

nodes.name: Melee tactic selection
nodes.purpose: Selects scripted fight tactic tables from distance and facing, queues up to six actions, computes weapon reach and gates finishing moves.

nodes.name: Projectiles and collision rays
nodes.purpose: Spawns arrows and spells, integrates gravity along their flight, sweeps them against characters and level geometry, reflects them off hard surfaces and retires them by impact count or path length.

cards.name: Orbit distance and zoom steps
cards.summary: The third-person camera stores zoom as a fraction from 0 to 1, expands it through the active preset's authored distance range and moves it by a fixed step per wheel notch.
cards.behavior: Zoom is not an absolute length. Each camera preset authors a minimum, a maximum and a preferred orbit distance. The controller keeps one fraction between zero and one that selects a point inside the active preset's span. Switching between two ordinary gameplay modes keeps the fraction. Any other mode change, such as entering or leaving a cutscene or first person, rebuilds the fraction from the preferred distance of the new preset. Each wheel event moves the fraction by one fixed step, only the sign of the wheel delta matters, and the result is clamped. First person ignores wheel zoom. On every camera update the fraction is expanded into the preset span. The third-person solver multiplies that span value by one hundred to get world units, which are centimetres. A dialog camera skips both the fraction and the scale and uses a distance that the dialog system sets directly. The orbit distance is not smoothed on its own. The camera position follows the requested orbit through a follow solver, and only when the preset enables position following. The projection uses a ten-unit near plane and a hundred-thousand-unit far plane. This is the OpenGothic reimplementation of the original camera, so the preset values come from the game scripts.

constants.name: Zoom step
constants.unit: fraction of the preset minimum-to-maximum orbit distance per wheel event; applied immediately, one step per input event

constants.name: Range unit scale
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per authored camera-range unit, applied on every non-dialog camera update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Near clipping distance
constants.unit: centimetres from the eye, applied per rendered frame, rate unverified

constants.name: Far clipping distance
constants.unit: centimetres from the eye (one kilometre), applied per rendered frame, rate unverified

capabilities: normalized zoom shared across camera presets
mode switches that restore the preferred distance
near and far planes sized for a large outdoor world

cards.name: Camera pull-in and the close-wall lift
cards.summary: A 3x3 grid of rays shortens the orbit before it crosses geometry and keeps a fixed clearance. When the remaining distance is too short the camera is placed on a longer, steep overhead orbit instead.
cards.behavior: When the active preset enables camera collision, the third-person solver casts nine rays from the follow target. They pass through the center, edges and corners of the near plane of the desired view. Each hit is projected onto the orbit direction and reduced by a fixed clearance. The shortest result becomes the orbit distance, and it can only shorten the orbit. A smaller single-ray probe, with its own clearance of the same size, shortens the target offset when it points into geometry. After the shortening, if the orbit distance is below a low threshold, the solver replaces it with a longer distance and recomputes the camera direction from a steep elevation angle. A positive elevation here looks down at the target, which lifts the camera above the character when a wall is behind it. The final look angles are computed from the new camera position to the target, so the character stays framed. The code comment says the original game moves the camera up gradually. This reimplementation jumps to the lifted placement in one update. The solver runs on every camera update.

constants.name: Camera wall clearance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of clearance kept between the camera and a hit surface, applied on every camera update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Close-wall lift threshold
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of orbit distance after shortening; below this value the lift branch runs, checked on every camera update

constants.name: Lifted orbit distance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of orbit distance used by the lift branch, applied on every update while the branch is active

constants.name: Lifted elevation
constants.unit: degrees of elevation used by the lift branch, applied on every update while the branch is active; a positive value looks down at the target

cards.name: Pitch limits, look-back and the first-person eye
cards.summary: Orbit spin is clamped to an elevation band and a full-turn azimuth band that is measured from the character's yaw. Look-back and first person select separate presets, and first person puts the eye 20 units forward of the head bone.
cards.behavior: The clamp subtracts the character's yaw from the camera yaw before limiting, so the azimuth limit follows the body while the character turns. The elevation limit is not relative to the body, because the body only has a yaw. Elevation is clamped between a lower and an upper value. A positive elevation looks down from above, inferred from the lift branch of the orbit solver. The azimuth limit is a half turn either way, so it does not restrict a full circle in practice. Holding look-back selects the preset authored for that view and wins over first person. The first-person mode starts from the character's yaw at the moment of entry. After that it uses the spin that mouse input has accumulated, with the same clamp. The eye is the head-bone transform of the character with a forward offset of 20 units, or the root transform when the head bone is missing. Entering or leaving first person is a mode change that is not between two ordinary modes, so the orbit distance resets to the preferred value of the regular preset on return. Wheel zoom is ignored in first person. The clamp runs on each camera update.

constants.name: Maximum elevation
constants.unit: degrees of camera spin elevation, an absolute limit that is not relative to the body, clamped on every camera update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Minimum elevation
constants.unit: degrees of camera spin elevation, an absolute limit that is not relative to the body, clamped on every camera update

constants.name: Azimuth limit
constants.unit: degrees to either side of the character's yaw, clamped on every camera update

constants.name: First-person eye offset
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) forward of the head bone in first person, applied on every first-person camera update

capabilities: absolute elevation clamp and body-relative azimuth clamp

cards.name: Body turn rate with and without a weapon
cards.summary: Keyboard turning is a fixed angular rate that doubles when any weapon state is active. It is blocked in some body states, and turn animations are limited by a 30 degrees-per-second threshold and a cooldown.
cards.behavior: When rotation is allowed, each left or right input adds a rate multiplied by the elapsed seconds. The rate is 90 degrees per second with no weapon state and 180 degrees per second in every other weapon state: fists, one-handed, two-handed, bow, crossbow and spell. A source comment says other references give 100 and 200 and that the OpenGothic author measured 90 and 180, so these are reimplementation values. Mouse turning adds the raw mouse angle in the same update and has no rate cap. Manual turning is skipped while the action key is held. The rotation gate also refuses an active object interaction, a finishing move, climbing, lying and a deep fall. A turn animation is requested only when the angle change per second needed to reach the wanted facing exceeds 30 degrees per second, unless a turn key is held, which forces the request. After a request, switching to a different turn animation, or clearing it, waits for a 100 ms cooldown. Repeating the animation that is already active is always allowed.

constants.name: Unarmed turn rate
constants.unit: degrees per second with no weapon state, integrated on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Armed turn rate
constants.unit: degrees per second in every weapon state other than no weapon, integrated on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Turn-animation threshold
constants.unit: degrees per second of required facing change; below this no turn animation is started unless forced, checked on each update

constants.name: Turn-animation cooldown
constants.unit: milliseconds of game time before the turn animation may change to a different one, checked on each update unless forced

capabilities: mouse turn applied without a rate cap

cards.name: Run lean and automatic facing in combat
cards.summary: A running character leans toward the camera's yaw offset, up to 14.5 degrees. Holding the action key or strafing makes the body turn toward the current target at the guild turn speed, doubled while the action key is held.
cards.behavior: While the character runs in run mode, the controller reads the camera azimuth. That value is the difference between the orbit's requested yaw and the camera's actual look yaw. It is clamped to 14.5 degrees either way and becomes the lean destination. The destination eases toward the clamped value with a factor of five per second, capped at one per update. Outside run mode the destination eases toward zero. The applied lean then moves toward the destination at 35 degrees per second. Auto-facing runs when the action key is held, when a strafe animation is active or during a finishing move. It needs a current target. With no weapon state, or during a finishing move, the target is cleared instead, so no turn happens. An attack animation also blocks the turn. Otherwise the body rotates toward the target using the guild turn speed from the game scripts, and that speed doubles while the action key is held.

constants.name: Run lean cap
constants.unit: degrees of lean to either side, clamped on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Visible lean rate
constants.unit: degrees per second at which the applied lean approaches its destination, integrated on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Lean destination smoothing
constants.unit: inverse seconds, exponential factor with the per-update blend capped at 1, applied on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Combat auto-turn multiplier
constants.unit: multiple of the guild turn speed applied while the action key is held, evaluated on each update

cards.name: Movement distance comes from animation root motion
cards.summary: Walk, run, sneak, swim and dive are separate clip families. The distance a character moves comes from the root-bone translation of the playing clip between two animation times, not from a speed table.
cards.behavior: The animation solver chooses a clip family from the walk mode: dive, swim, sneak, walk or run. It then picks the clip for the requested action, such as forward, left strafe, right strafe or backward. Swim and dive strafe requests fall back to the plain swim or dive clip, and a missing backward clip falls back to a jump-back clip. When a clip loads, its root-node samples are compared with the first sample. The clip is marked as moving if any axis offset reaches the threshold at any frame. Each update, the pose asks the top-most active layer that has root movement for the root offset at the current animation time and at one step later. The difference is the movement delta for that update, and a looping clip carries its total offset across loops. A reversed clip negates the delta. Only the horizontal part is used for walking. The vertical part is used for climbing. Because the delta carries the authored pace of the clip, the same code produces a sneak, a walk and a run without a speed table. When an AI character goes to a point or another character, the horizontal delta is scaled down so the step cannot be longer than the remaining distance. The scaling is skipped when the squared step is below a small floor. A comment in the source marks the choice of the earlier time sample as probably more correct, so this is a reimplementation choice.

constants.name: Root-motion detection threshold
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of root-bone offset from the first sampled frame on any axis; evaluated once per clip at load, over the frames of the clip at its authored frame rate

constants.name: Approach-speed floor
constants.unit: squared world units of the per-update horizontal step; below this the step is not scaled, checked on each locomotion update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

capabilities: locomotion clip chosen by movement mode
displacement sampled between two animation times
approach step shortened near the destination

cards.name: Step height, ground stick and wall rejection
cards.summary: Ground detection snaps a grounded character onto floor that is lower by up to the guild step height. Airborne characters get no such tolerance, and a steep slope blocks moves that do not point downhill.
cards.behavior: Each locomotion update reads a downward ground ray. The result is cached until the character has moved more than a small tolerance on any axis. The ray starts a little above the feet. The step height comes from the guild table and falls back to 50 world units when that value is zero or negative. While the character is grounded, the step height is the stick tolerance. If the floor is lower than the feet by no more than that tolerance, or is slightly above the feet, the body moves onto the floor and the state returns to running. While falling, in a jump-up or in the air, the tolerance is zero, so a nearby ledge cannot cancel a fall. When the floor is further away than the tolerance, the character starts to fall. In walk mode, the player never steps off such an edge. A non-player character in walk mode refuses it when the drop is at least three quarters of the guild fall height. The move is undone and the blocked-move recovery runs. This is how a walking character stops at a ledge, while a running character falls. On a slope steeper than the guild slide angle, a character that is not airborne is blocked when the dot product of its move step and the surface normal is below a small value. Otherwise it enters the slide state. While airborne, the vertical speed is compared with a threshold to choose the short-fall clip. The deep-fall clip is chosen when the drop height, computed from the vertical speed alone, exceeds the guild fall height.

constants.name: Default step height
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of vertical step used on each locomotion update when the guild table value is zero or negative; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Ground ray cache tolerance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of movement per axis before a cached ray is cast again, checked on each update

constants.name: Wall rejection threshold
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per update of the move step projected on the surface normal; below this a non-airborne move on a slippery slope is refused, checked on each update

constants.name: Short-fall speed threshold
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per millisecond of vertical speed; values below -0.3 select the ordinary fall clip, checked on each airborne update

cards.name: Jump probe and ledge climb bands
cards.summary: A standing jump first probes 55 units ahead. If the way is blocked, the ledge height picks a low footstep, a hand-supported climb or a jump up that hangs and then pulls up, with a launch speed that reaches the guild jump height.
cards.behavior: A standing jump calls the probe. It sweeps the body 55 units forward along the facing. If the sweep is free, a normal jump follows. If it is blocked, a ray cast from above the obstacle finds the ledge height, and the rise from the feet to that height picks the response. A rise that is zero or negative, or a blocked path onto the ledge, gives a plain jump-up with no climb. A rise up to the guild low height gives a large footstep. A rise up to the guild middle height gives a climb with hand support. A taller rise starts a jump up. The jump-up targets the feet height plus the guild jump-up height, so the guild jump-up height sets how high the launch reaches and the middle height is the boundary. During the rise the probe runs again. When the ledge is within the low height plus the animation offset, the rise stops, the climb state starts and the character hangs and pulls up. If no ledge appears, the character falls. The launch speed is the speed that reaches the wanted rise under gravity with no vertical speed left at the top. That is the square root of two times gravity times the rise. The pull-up uses the root motion of the clip. When the climb ends, the character is placed 55 units forward of the climb start, at the ledge height. A jump while wading in water, when standing, skips the probe and starts a jump up to the guild jump-up height. A jump while swimming starts a dive instead. This is the OpenGothic reimplementation of the original behavior.

constants.name: Ledge probe distance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) ahead of the feet for the jump probe and the final climb step; evaluated once per jump attempt or climb exit

constants.name: Launch-speed rise factor
constants.unit: dimensionless factor in the launch time, the square root of twice the rise over gravity; launch speed is gravity times that time; computed once per climb start

capabilities: three climb responses by ledge height
climb exit snapped onto the ledge
water jump using the guild jump height

cards.name: Wall bounce and sidestep recovery
cards.summary: When a step is refused, the character may try rotated moves in 5 degree steps up to 35 degrees. Otherwise a forward move turns toward the freer side at 360 degrees per second. A cooldown for non-player characters limits how often the rotated moves run.
cards.behavior: A refused move first measures the sideways part of the surface normal relative to the move direction. If its magnitude is at least the bounce threshold, the hit is a glancing one. The move is not a pre-fall refusal, and the bounce cooldown has expired. Then the code tries the move rotated by five degrees, then minus five, then ten, and so on up to thirty-five degrees on both sides. The first rotated move that passes the collision test is used. A forward move also rotates the body by the tested angle. The source comment says this emulates the bouncing of the original game. If no rotated move passes, or the cooldown is active, and the move is a forward one, the body turns toward the side given by the sign of the sideways normal part, at 360 degrees per second. An attack animation blocks this turn unless the refusal was a ledge refusal. When the hit is head-on, the result depends on the script hint for the movement. With no movement hint the character goes idle. An AI character with a hint may turn, clear its path or try a climb. The cooldown is set only for characters that the player does not control, 800 ms after hitting another character and 750 ms after hitting level geometry. A move counts as forward when its direction is within about 37 degrees of the facing.

constants.name: Bounce threshold
constants.unit: dimensionless magnitude of the sideways part of the unit hit normal relative to the move direction; checked on each blocked move

constants.name: Recovery turn rate
constants.unit: degrees per second of corrective body turn, integrated on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Character bounce cooldown
constants.unit: milliseconds of game time added to the bounce clock after hitting another character; applies only to non-player characters, checked on each blocked move

constants.name: Geometry bounce cooldown
constants.unit: milliseconds of game time added to the bounce clock after hitting level geometry; applies only to non-player characters, checked on each blocked move

constants.name: Probe angle step
constants.unit: degrees between candidate directions in the recovery fan, tested on each blocked move

capabilities: fixed-rate turn along a blocking wall
separate cooldowns for characters and geometry

cards.name: Impact-speed fall damage
cards.summary: Landing damage is rebuilt from the impact speed as an equivalent drop height. The guild safe height is subtracted and the rest is multiplied by the guild damage per metre.
cards.behavior: While airborne, the locomotion solver adds gravity to the fall velocity on each update. On landing from the air or a deep fall, the full length of the velocity vector, including any horizontal part, goes to the damage calculator. The calculator divides the speed by gravity to get a fall time, then forms the height as one half of gravity times that time squared. This equals the speed squared over twice the gravity, so damage depends on impact speed and not on the simulated fall length. The guild safe fall height is subtracted, the remainder in world units is divided by one hundred to get metres, and the result is multiplied by the guild damage per metre. The flat fall protection value is then subtracted and the sum is cut to an integer. A negative protection value marks the character as immune. A result of zero or less means no hit. Only a hit lowers health. In the air, a separate check of the vertical speed alone picks the deep-fall clip when the drop height exceeds the safe height. On landing from a deep fall, one of two landing clips is chosen. The first is used when the horizontal impact speed is tiny or the motion points along the body's facing. The second is used otherwise. The gravity constant is stored in world units per millisecond squared.

constants.name: Gravity
constants.unit: metres per second squared, stored as world units (centimetres) per millisecond squared and integrated on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Height coefficient
constants.unit: dimensionless coefficient of gravity times fall time squared, evaluated once at landing

constants.name: Centimetres per metre
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per metre, used once at landing to convert the excess height

capabilities: fall damage derived from impact speed
deep-fall animation and landing pose selection

cards.name: Glancing blows and the damage floor
cards.summary: A melee hit rolls against a script hit chance. In the second game a failed roll cuts each damage type to one tenth, and any hit that was not blocked as immune is raised to a minimum of five. The first game uses a critical multiplier.
cards.behavior: For a fist, one-handed or two-handed attack, the calculator builds a damage type mask from the active weapon, or from the character if it holds none. For each type in the mask, it adds the attacker's strength to the attacker's damage value for that type and subtracts the defender's protection for that type. The result is cut at zero. A random roll from zero to ninety-nine is compared with the hit chance for the weapon class from the script tables. In the second game, a roll below the hit chance gives full damage. A roll equal to or above it reduces each type to one tenth, using integer division after subtracting one. A monster without a weapon talent skips the roll and always deals full damage. A type with negative protection is immune and adds nothing. If every type is immune, the hit is marked invincible. In the first game, the roll below the talent value multiplies the weapon part of the damage by the script critical multiplier. After the types are summed in the second game, any hit that is not invincible is raised to a floor of five health. That floor also covers arrows and spells.

constants.name: Talent roll ceiling
constants.unit: count of possible values of the per-hit random roll, from 0 to 99, drawn once per melee hit

constants.name: Glancing damage divisor
constants.unit: divisor applied to each damage type on a failed roll, drawn once per melee hit

constants.name: Minimum damage
constants.unit: health points, floor applied after mitigation on any hit that is not invincible in the second game, once per hit

capabilities: hit-chance roll with a one-tenth damage penalty
strength plus weapon damage before armour

cards.name: Bow hit chance falloff
cards.summary: An arrow always connects at point blank. The chance falls to the archer's stored chance at a reference range, then to zero at the maximum range.
cards.behavior: The calculator starts from the path length that the projectile has flown, not from the straight distance between shooter and target. The hit chance is built in two segments. Closer than the reference range, it blends from one at zero distance to the archer's stored chance at the reference range. Between the reference range and the maximum range it blends from the stored chance to zero. Beyond the maximum range it is zero. A random roll from zero to ninety-nine, divided by one hundred, is compared with this value. The shot misses when the chance is less than or equal to the roll. The stored chance is set at the shot. In the second game it is the script hit chance for the bow or crossbow talent. In the first game it is the dexterity attribute. In the first game a second roll against the bow talent may multiply the damage by the script critical multiplier, and the first game uses a longer reference range. After a hit, the damage flags from the collision double or halve the damage first. Then each damage type is reduced by the target's protection. Spells skip this curve and are limited by a separate magic range instead.

constants.name: Second-game reference range
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of projectile path at which the hit chance equals the archer's stored chance; evaluated once per shot

constants.name: Maximum bow range
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of projectile path beyond which the hit chance is zero; evaluated once per shot

constants.name: First-game reference range
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of projectile path at which the hit chance equals the archer's stored chance; evaluated once per shot

constants.name: Hit roll ceiling
constants.unit: count of possible values of the per-shot random roll, from 0 to 99, drawn once per shot

capabilities: hit chance from projectile path length

cards.name: Melee reach, facing cone and finishing distance
cards.summary: Melee reach is both fighters' guild base reach plus a guild reach for the weapon class and the blade length. A 30 degree focus cone chooses the fight plan. An unconscious target inside the finishing distance can be killed with a finishing move.
cards.behavior: This logic lives in the fight AI and is also used by the player's range tests. There is no single global range. The attack range is the sum of the guild base reach of both fighters and the attacker's weapon reach. The weapon reach is a guild value for the weapon class plus the blade length for one-handed and two-handed weapons. Fists use a guild fist reach. A bow uses the reference bow range, and a spell uses the magic range. A separate group range adds a guild group value. Distances are compared as squared distances between the character root positions. The fight plan table of the script is chosen from the range and focus tests. A target inside the 30 degree half-angle of the attacker's facing counts as in focus. Being in focus, and whether the character is running, picks a run-to or a focus plan. A plan holds at most six queued actions. A target closer than three quarters of the combined base reach is in close-up range. When it is also in focus and the plan says wait or turn, the character jumps back. Separately, a jump-back animation negates a hit that comes from within a 90 degree half-angle of the facing. A finishing move needs a one-handed or two-handed weapon and an unconscious target. The distance must be inside the finishing distance, which defaults to 180 units and can be overridden by a script symbol. The move sets the target's health to zero and sends a murder perception to nearby characters.

constants.name: Finishing distance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) between character roots for a finishing move, checked on each finishing attempt; a script symbol can override it

constants.name: Focus half-angle
constants.unit: degrees of half-angle, giving a 60 degree facing cone; checked on each combat instruction

constants.name: Back-jump half-angle
constants.unit: degrees of half-angle, giving a 180 degree arc in which a jump-back negates an incoming hit; checked on each incoming hit

constants.name: Close-up range fraction
constants.unit: fraction of the combined guild base reach; at or below this distance the close-up branch applies, checked on each combat instruction

constants.name: Combat queue depth
constants.unit: count of queued actions per fight plan, resolved on each instruction fetch

cards.name: Arrow gravity, ricochet and lifetime
cards.summary: Arrows fly at 3 units per millisecond with an aimed lead and gravity. They bounce off stone and metal at half speed and stop on other surfaces. Spells fly at 1 unit per millisecond, ignore gravity and stop on the first surface.
cards.behavior: Arrows start at the weapon bone with the arrow speed. Spells start at the caster's collision center, or at an effect bone, or at the weapon bone when there is no target, and use the spell speed. For an arrow aimed at a target or an interactive object, the horizontal distance divided by the speed gives a flight time. The aim vector is divided by that time, so its horizontal part has the arrow speed. Half of gravity times the flight time is then added to the vertical part. This lead approximately cancels the drop. On each update, the projectile checks the swept segment against characters first through their boxes. It then ray-tests the level. An arrow adds a gravity step to its vertical speed each update and also lowers its position by a gravity term. A spell does neither. A level hit on stone or metal reflects the arrow about the surface normal and keeps half the speed. A hit shorter than a tenth of a unit is ignored. Any other surface stops the arrow at once, and a spell stops on any surface. A projectile is retired after more than three impacts or after ten thousand units of accumulated path, so a long ricochet ends.

constants.name: Arrow speed
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per millisecond, which is 30 metres per second, applied on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Spell speed
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) per millisecond, which is 10 metres per second, applied on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Ricochet speed factor
constants.unit: fraction of the speed kept after a stone or metal impact; applied once per impact

constants.name: Gravity lead factor
constants.unit: fraction of gravity times the flight time, added to the vertical aim speed; computed once per shot

constants.name: Projectile path cap
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of accumulated projectile path, which is 100 metres, before retirement; checked on each update

constants.name: Projectile impact cap
constants.unit: count of impacts above which a projectile is retired; checked on each impact

capabilities: ballistic lead for a moving target point
gravity applied to arrows but not spells
retirement by impact count or path length

cards.name: Wading, swimming and the dive timer
cards.summary: Water depth over the ground is compared with guild knee and chest depths. Knee depth starts wading, chest depth starts swimming at the surface, and diving is locked for one second after each dive change.
cards.behavior: Water interaction uses two guild depths, a knee depth and a chest depth, measured as the water surface height over the ground. If the ground is above the water, nothing changes. When the water reaches the knee depth but not the chest depth, the character wades and uses the wading walk clips. When the water reaches the chest depth and the character has swim animations, the character enters the swim state. The body is then held so that its chest rides at the surface. On entering swim, weapons other than fists are sheathed and a torch is dropped, and a splash starts when the entry was fast. A character without swim animations refuses to walk into water that deep. A creature whose two depths both carry the fly-over hint stays on the surface instead. A dive request works only from swim and only more than one second after the last dive start or end. Entering dive pitches the body to minus forty degrees. While diving, if the chest rises above the surface, the body is moved down to chest depth, and if more than two seconds have passed since the dive began, the state returns to swim. Staying under water longer than the guild dive time, in seconds, starts periodic drowning damage. The scripts set the interval, and one health point is taken per elapsed interval. This is the OpenGothic reimplementation of the original water rules.

constants.name: Swim trigger tolerance
constants.unit: world units (centimetres) of tolerance above the water level for the swim trigger, checked on each update; the update step is clamped to 5-50 ms

constants.name: Dive re-entry lockout
